characters: Zaara: an eight-year-old Ghanaian girl in a neat blue-and-yellow school uniform and tidy white headscarf, holding a red-and-blue magnet.
Worla: her eight-year-old male classmate with short neat hair in a matching yellow uniform shirt and blue shorts, holding an exercise book and pencil.
Madam Salamatu: their warm Ghanaian class teacher wearing a bright emerald-and-gold African-print dress.

narrationPlan.voice: An excited voice for Zaara; a calm voice for Worla; a kind, clear teacher voice for Madam Salamatu
narrationPlan.pace: Curious and clear, with a crisp click for each pull (about 90 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A light bouncing tune with a small click sound for each pull (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Magnets appear in many Ghanaian classrooms and homes—for example inside refrigerator door seals and radio speakers.
The safety warning against putting magnets near the mouth or leaving them near toddlers is essential classroom guidance.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Confirm that classroom paper clips and pins used in demonstrations are steel rather than brass or plastic-coated aluminium.
Confirm that the magnet safety message is clear, calm, and age-appropriate.

teacherGuide.overview: A hands-on classroom magnet investigation showing that magnets attract iron and steel, leave non-magnetic materials unmoved, act through thin paper, and either attract or repel another magnet.
learningGoals: Sort everyday objects into magnetic and non-magnetic.
Demonstrate that opposite magnet ends pull together and matching ends push apart.
State why magnets must never go near the mouth or small children.
beforeReading: Hold up a magnet and ask learners to predict which items on your table it will pick up.
whileReading: Pause on page 3 to emphasize that not every shiny metal is magnetic (for example, aluminium foil).
afterReading: Test eight safe classroom objects in pairs and draw them in two picture columns.
Count how many magnets the teacher hands out and count them all back into the storage box.
discussion: Why do we count and lock away magnets after science class?
reflection: How do you help keep science tools safe in your classroom?

support: Provide four safe test items per group and sort them onto two coloured trays.
stretch: Predict first, then test whether a magnet can pull a paper clip through card, cloth, and a thin book.

culturalNotes: Magnets appear in many Ghanaian classrooms and homes—for example inside refrigerator door seals and radio speakers.
The safety warning against putting magnets near the mouth or leaving them near toddlers is essential classroom guidance.
localiseThis: Point out everyday magnets in radio speakers, handbag clasps, and fridge doors.
Always store strong magnets out of reach of younger siblings and toddlers.

factCheck.claim: Magnets attract iron and steel rather than aluminium, wood, plastic, or glass, and opposite poles attract while like poles repel.
factCheck.explanation: Ferromagnetic metals such as iron and steel respond strongly to magnetic fields, whereas everyday aluminium, wood, plastic, and glass do not.
factCheck.reference: NaCCA Ghana Primary Integrated Science Curriculum (Forces and Magnets)
